parts.title: A morning on the river
parts.instructions: Read the article and choose the best answer for each question.
parts.passage:
Every Saturday, my grandfather takes me fishing on the river near his village. We leave at five, when it is still dark, and we walk for twenty minutes along a muddy path. He says that the fish are most hungry at dawn.

I used to find fishing boring. You sit for hours, and often you catch nothing. But last summer, I began to understand why my grandfather loves it. Sitting by the water, you notice small things: a kingfisher flashing blue across the river, or an otter swimming near the bank. Grandfather taught me to keep still and listen.

One morning, I felt a strong pull on my line. I held on with both hands, and after ten minutes, I lifted a huge fish out of the water. It was nearly as long as my arm! Grandfather smiled and said, "Now put it back." I was surprised, but he explained that big fish are the mothers, and the river needs them.

I let it go, and it disappeared with a flick of its tail. I felt a little sad, but also proud. That was the best catch of my life, even though I did not take it home.

questions.explanation: He says that the fish are most hungry at dawn.

questions.explanation: She noticed a kingfisher and an otter.

parts.title: Rivers around the world
parts.instructions: Choose the sentence that fits each gap. There are three extra sentences.
parts.passage:
Rivers have always been important for people. [1] The earliest cities grew up beside great rivers, because the land there was good for farming.

A river starts as a small stream high in the mountains. [2] As it moves downhill, more streams join it, and it becomes wider and stronger.

Many rivers carry boats and goods. [3] Before roads and railways, it was often the fastest way to travel from one town to another.

Rivers are also home to many animals. [4] Otters, fish and birds all depend on clean water to survive.

Unfortunately, some rivers are becoming polluted. [5] If we want to keep them healthy, everyone must help to protect them.
sentences: Ships and barges can carry heavy loads over long distances.
Bridges were built wherever the river was narrow.
Hundreds of tourists swim in it every summer.
Rain and melting snow feed it from the beginning.
Fishing is a popular hobby in many countries.
They supplied water for drinking, washing and growing food.
Factories and farms sometimes pour waste into the water.
Some species live nowhere else on Earth.

gaps.explanation: Rivers supplied water and food, and the next sentence says early cities grew beside them.
Rain and snow feed the stream; the next sentence says more streams join it.
Ships carry heavy loads, and the next sentence says it was the fastest way before roads.
Some species live nowhere else; the next sentence lists otters, fish and birds.
Waste is poured into the water, which causes pollution; the next sentence says we must protect rivers.

parts.title: A day's fishing
parts.instructions: Write one word in each gap.
parts.passage: Fishing is a hobby that needs a lot of patience. You often have to wait for hours [1] a fish bites. Most people use a long rod with a line and a hook, and they put a small piece of food, called bait, on the end. [2] you want to catch a certain kind of fish, you must choose the right bait. For example, worms are good for river fish, [3] bread is popular for fish in lakes. In many countries, you need a permit [4] fish legally. If you catch a very small fish, you should always put it back [5] the water. Finally, remember to take all your rubbish home. Fishermen love beautiful places, and they want to keep them clean [6] everyone to enjoy.

gaps.explanation: You wait until a fish bites: the moment it happens.
If you want to catch a certain fish, you must choose the right bait.
The sentence contrasts bait for river fish with bait for lake fish.
A permit to fish gives the purpose.
You put the fish back into the water.
Clean for everyone to enjoy: the purpose.

parts.title: A welcome at Lakeside Fishing Day
parts.instructions: Listen to the talk and complete each note. Write one or two words, a number, a date or a time.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Good morning, everyone, and welcome to Lakeside Fishing Day. My name is Ziv. First, let me explain the rules. Last year people could take home four fish, but the lake is smaller now, so you may keep up to two fish. If you catch more, please put them back. Also think about size. Fish smaller than ten centimetres are babies, and for the tiny kind the law says fifteen, but for the fish in this lake the minimum is twenty centimetres. We have rulers on every table. Now the timetable. Breakfast is at six, but fishing doesn’t start then. Some people ask to begin earlier, because the fish are active at dawn, but the council doesn’t allow it. You can put your lines in the water at seven o’clock, and we stop at noon. Next, buckets. You will find buckets at every place. The blue ones are for water and the green ones are for bait, so please don’t mix them. The fish you want to keep go in the red buckets. Remember to change the water in them every hour. Where to fish? Many people stay near the dock, because it is easy to reach, but the fish there are small. The best fish usually bite near the old tree on the north side, where the water is deeper and it’s shady. It takes ten minutes to walk there. Finally, if you need help, look for the guides. We wear orange jackets, so you can see us from far away. Last year our jackets were yellow, but that confused people, because the safety staff wear yellow. So now we are orange. If you have any problem, put your hand up and we’ll come. Right, let’s get started! Pick up a rod and a bucket, and enjoy the day.

gaps.prompt: Visitors may keep up to ___ fish
gaps.explanation: Four fish was last year’s limit; now they may keep two.

gaps.prompt: Fish must be longer than ___ centimetres
gaps.explanation: Ten and fifteen are other sizes; for this lake the minimum is twenty centimetres.
Breakfast is at six but the lines go in the water at seven.

gaps.prompt: Fish that visitors keep go in the ___ buckets
gaps.explanation: Blue buckets are for water and green for bait; the fish go in the red ones.

gaps.prompt: The best fish usually bite near the old ___
gaps.explanation: The dock is easy to reach but has small fish; the best are near the old tree.
Last year the jackets were yellow, but the safety staff wear yellow, so now they are orange.

parts.title: An interview with a river ranger
parts.instructions: Listen to the interview and choose the correct answer.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: Cyd, you work on the river every day. What does your job involve?

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: People imagine I sell fishing permits all day, and my colleague in the office does that. I’m not a swimming teacher either, although I’m happy when children learn. What I do is walk along the bank in the morning, test the water and count the fish. It sounds simple, but it takes hours, and I write everything in a notebook that is almost falling apart.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: What is the biggest problem for the river?

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: Noise isn’t a problem, and floods happen once or twice a year, but the water goes down again and the river recovers. What worries me every day is plastic: bottles, bags, bits of fishing line. It stays in the water for years and animals eat it. I find more every spring.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: Why are visitors surprised when they see the river?

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: Because otters live there again. Twenty years ago there were none, and the water was too dirty. Now it’s clean enough, and a family of otters has made a home under the old bridge. People expect to see big fish, but the fish are normal size. The otters are the surprise, and children love them. Last month a school came and sat on the bank for two hours with binoculars, completely silent.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: How can people help?

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: It’s easy. We don’t need more boats, the river is busy enough. And I’d say fish less, not more, in the summer, when the water is warm. The best thing is to take your rubbish home with you. If everybody did that, my job would be so much easier.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: What did you see last week?

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: Something beautiful. I wasn’t lucky with a huge fish and I haven’t seen a rare frog this year. But I stood very still by the bridge, and a kingfisher dived right in front of me, blue and orange, and came up with a tiny fish. I felt so lucky that I forgot my notebook.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: Why is autumn your favourite season?

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: Many people choose summer, and spring is lovely with the flowers. But autumn is quiet. The visitors go home, the leaves fall on the water, and I can walk for hours and meet nobody. I have the whole river to myself, and that’s what I like.

options: Checks the water and counts fish
questions.explanation: She says she does not sell permits or teach swimming; she tests the water and counts the fish.

questions.prompt: What is the biggest problem for the river?
questions.explanation: Noise is not a problem and floods pass; the plastic stays in the water for years and animals eat it.
